explanations.answer: He will not let Samson enter
explanations.explanation: Samson, an Israelite, shows up at his wife's home and says, “I want to go to my wife in her room…” But her father would not let him enter. That door stays shut, friend. Whatever Samson pictured for this visit, I bet it didn't start with a closed door.

explanations.answer: He calls his daughter to the door
explanations.explanation: The text never has the wife come to the door. It says her father would not let Samson enter. So Samson came all this way to see her and gets her dad instead. I think that's the least fun swap in the whole story.

explanations.answer: He sends Samson out to the fields
explanations.explanation: Harvest time is when Samson comes, but nobody hands him a sickle and points him outside. The father simply would not let him enter. The door stays closed, and that's the whole answer.

Her father asks, “Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she?” Then he says, “Please take her instead.” I think he's trying to make things right on the spot. Friend, it's like a bakery handing you a different batch when you came for the one you ordered.

Thirty linen garments come from Samson's wedding feast riddle (Judges 14:12). They aren't what her father offers here. In this scene, he offers Samson her younger sister. Same story, different moment.
It is wheat harvest time, so I see how that one sneaks in. But her father never mentions wheat. He offers Samson her younger sister instead. Nobody is bargaining over grain at that door.

explanations.answer: He will be blameless in doing it
explanations.explanation: Samson says, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines.” Later the men of Judah tell him the Philistines rule over them (Judges 15:11). Notice he says “this time.” I think he feels the door slammed in his face, and he's done being polite.

explanations.answer: He will ask the LORD first
explanations.explanation: Samson says nothing about asking the LORD first in this speech. The text only has him say he will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines. When he does speak to the LORD, it comes at the end of the passage (Judges 15:18). Different moment, different words.

explanations.answer: He will wait until the harvest ends
explanations.explanation: Waiting is not in this speech at all. Samson says, “This time I will be blameless in doing harm to the Philistines.” Then he goes out and gets moving. This man does not check the calendar.
Samson turns the foxes tail-to-tail and fastens a torch between each pair of tails. That's the whole setup. Three hundred foxes and all those torches is a lot of prep, friend.
Rope shows up later in this passage, but not here. Between each pair of fox tails Samson fastens a torch. The torches are the point of the whole plan.
Ruby, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like a bell, and she is LOUD. But no bells on these foxes. Samson fastens a torch between each pair of tails.

Samson lit the torches and released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines. The grain was standing out in the fields, ready for harvest. That's where the fire starts. And that is a very bad day for a harvest.
Ashkelon is a Philistine city that Samson visited once before (Judges 14:19). But here the foxes go into the standing grain. The fields are the target, not the city streets.

explanations.answer: Into the hill country of Judah
explanations.explanation: Judah is one of Israel's tribes, and the men of Judah show up later in this passage. The text says Samson released the foxes into the standing grain of the Philistines. So the fire goes into the Philistines' grain, and Judah isn't named as where it goes.

The text says the fire burned up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves. So the vineyards and olive groves are on the burned list too. That's a long list of burned places, friend.

That's right. The fire burned up the piles of grain and the standing grain, as well as the vineyards and olive groves. It didn't stop at the grain. The text lists the vineyards and olive groves right along with it.

Yes. After the Philistines burned his wife and her father to death, Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you.” That is a heavy moment, friend. I think this is where the story turns very dark.

The text says the opposite. Samson told them, “Because you have done this, I will not rest until I have taken vengeance upon you.” This comes right after they burned his wife and her father to death. It's a heavy part of the story, and I won't pretend it's light.

After striking down the Philistines, Samson went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam. The text doesn't say why he stayed there, so I won't guess. Later, the men of Judah go to that very cave to find him.
No tent here. The text says Samson stayed in a cave at the rock of Etam. A tent is a very different kind of address, friend.
Samson goes down, not up. The text says he went down and stayed in the cave at the rock of Etam. A tower is up, a cave is down, and the verse says down, friend.

The Philistines say, “We have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to us.” So the army parks near Lehi and names its reason. And Judah, the tribe being camped on, is stuck in the middle of it.
Warning isn't what they came for. They say they have come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to them. That's a lot of army for a warning label.
Nobody's handing out a job offer here. The Philistines say they've come to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he has done to them. They came for payback and not a paycheck.

explanations.answer: He did to them what they did to him
explanations.explanation: Samson answers, “I have done to them what they did to me…” The men of Judah had asked, “What have you done to us?” and Samson doesn't dodge. He gives them one short answer. I think he figures it explains itself.

explanations.answer: The LORD told him to go after them
explanations.explanation: That's not what Samson says here. The text has him answer, “I have done to them what they did to me…” He doesn't mention the LORD sending him. We only know what he actually says.

explanations.answer: He is leaving Judah for good tomorrow
explanations.explanation: Samson makes no announcement about leaving. When the men of Judah ask what he has done to them, he says, “I have done to them what they did to me…” That's all. No packing, no goodbye tour.

Samson says to the men of Judah, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves.” They agree not to kill him, but they will tie him up and hand him over. So Samson gets one promise out of them. It's a small deal, but it's a deal.

The text says Samson does ask. He tells the men of Judah, “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves.” They answer that they will not kill him, but they will tie him up securely and hand him over. So he gets his promise, with strings attached. Literally.
They bound him with two new ropes and led him up from the rock. Two new ropes, friend. Not one, and the text says new.

Bowstrings, baker? You walked in with a whole archery shop. The text says the men of Judah bound Samson with two new ropes (Judges 15:13). They'd just promised not to kill him, and ropes were how they kept that promise and still handed him over. Then the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the ropes on his arms became like burnt flax (Judges 15:14). I bet seven bowstrings wouldn't have lasted any longer.
No metal in this scene. The text says the men of Judah bound Samson with two new ropes. Plain ropes, and brand new ones.

The text says the opposite. When the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon Samson, the ropes on his arms became like burnt flax. The bonds broke loose from his hands. Those new ropes did not hold, friend.
That's right. The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the ropes on his arms became like burnt flax. The bonds broke loose from his hands. The strength comes from the Spirit of the LORD.

explanations.answer: The fresh jawbone of a donkey
explanations.explanation: He found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it. Then he struck down a thousand men. That's what was lying there, and he took it. I'd have grabbed a rolling pin, friend, so I'm glad nobody asked me.

An ox goad is a pointed stick for driving oxen. Shamgar, son of Anath, struck down six hundred Philistines with one (Judges 3:31). But that's not what's in this verse. Here Samson finds the fresh jawbone of a donkey and takes it.
No tent peg here. The text says Samson found the fresh jawbone of a donkey, reached out his hand and took it. That's all he needed, friend.

When Samson had finished speaking, he cast the jawbone from his hand. Just before that he said, “With the jawbone of a donkey I have piled them into heaps.” Then he named that place Ramath-lehi. Speech finished, jawbone dropped, place named. That's a mic drop with paperwork, friend.

An altar? That's a holy thought, friend, but nobody in this scene is picking up a hammer. Samson has just struck down a thousand men with a jawbone, and then he casts it from his hand. The text says he names the place Ramath-lehi (Judges 15:17). Next thing he does is cry out to the LORD because he is very thirsty (Judges 15:18). I think a man that parched is looking for water, not building supplies.
The text says nothing about handing the place over to anyone. Samson casts the jawbone from his hand and names the spot Ramath-lehi. The only thing he gives this place is a name, friend.

explanations.answer: Whether he must now die of thirst
explanations.explanation: Samson cries out, “Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” He had just struck down a thousand men, and now he's asking about dying of thirst. I think he's worn out, friend. Honestly, I'd be asking the same thing.

explanations.answer: Whether he can go back home now
explanations.explanation: Going home isn't what he asks. Samson says, “Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” Thirst is the problem on his mind.
He doesn't ask about them coming back. His question is, “Must I now die of thirst and fall into the hands of the uncircumcised?” The worry he voices is his thirst.
God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. Samson cried out, and water came. That's about as plain as an answer gets.
Samson has met honey before (Judges 14:8-9), but that's not what comes out here. God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. Water was what a thirsty man needed.
Oil is a fine thing, but it won't help a thirsty man. The text says God opened up the hollow place in Lehi, and water came out of it. That's what Samson needed, so that's what came out.
The text says, “When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived.” He was worn out and thirsty, and the water changed that. That's the whole turnaround in a single verse.
The text says the opposite: “When Samson drank, his strength returned, and he was revived.” He was very thirsty before this. Then he drinks, and the text says his strength returned.
The text says Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines. A judge is a leader of Israel. Twenty years is a long stretch, friend.

Forty does show up earlier in Samson's story, where the LORD delivers Israel into the hands of the Philistines for forty years (Judges 13:1). But the number for Samson judging is a different one. The text says he judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines. Don't let those two numbers swap seats, friend.
Seven is a short stretch for this verse. The text says Samson judged Israel for twenty years in the days of the Philistines. That's a lot more than seven.
